title: Flash Report
summary: A flash report is a short, time-sensitive threat intelligence product published quickly to warn recipients about an urgent development and prompt a defensive decision. It is deliberately narrow: one topic, minimal background, and heavy emphasis on what changed, why it matters now, what recipients should do, and when the next update is expected. Flash traffic typically covers newly exploited vulnerabilities, active campaigns against a sector, credible reports of imminent activity, or a significant change in an adversary's tooling. Because speed is the point, a flash report is usually built from incomplete information, so it must state its confidence and its sourcing plainly, and it must be updated or formally superseded rather than silently edited after release. A workable structure includes a headline that states the change, a one-paragraph bottom line up front, key judgements with confidence, the technical detail analysts need in order to hunt, recommended actions ranked by effort and impact, indicators with a clear validity window, handling and distribution markings, and points of contact. Distribution is governed by handling caveats so recipients know whether they may forward the material, and by a defined list of who must be reachable outside business hours. The most common failure is noise: publishing everything urgently destroys the value of urgency, so teams set explicit triggers for what qualifies as flash and keep routine developments in a daily summary. The second failure is actionability, where a flash tells recipients that an actor exists without giving them a detection, a mitigation or a question to answer. Well-run teams keep a standing template, pre-agree who may approve release, and rehearse the workflow so a flash can be written, reviewed and distributed within an hour during an incident.
objectives: You will be able to identify the situations that genuinely meet a flash reporting trigger and those that belong in routine reporting.
You will be able to draft a flash report with a bottom line up front, stated confidence and ranked recommended actions.
You will be able to apply handling and distribution markings and explain what recipients may do with the product.
You will be able to convert technical findings into detection and hunting guidance a recipient can act on immediately.
You will be able to manage a flash lifecycle of publication, update, supersede and post-incident review.
You will be able to define release authority and out-of-hours routing so urgent warning is not delayed.
